title: How falling gas reshapes planet-forming discs
subtitle: From Anatomy of a Fall to AB Aurigae
description: How streams of fresh gas reshape planet-forming discs, from Anatomy of a Fall to the spirals around AB Aurigae.
summary: The discs where planets form can keep receiving gas from their surroundings. What happens when that fresh material arrives? In Anatomy of a Fall and my follow-up work on AB Aurigae, I explore how incoming streams create spiral arms and disturb the motion of gas—and how to recognise these effects in telescope observations.

thumbnail.alt: AB Aurigae observations on the left, compared with a simulation including infall and a proposed stellar companion on the right.
thumbnail.caption: AB Aurigae observed (left) and simulated (right). Calcino, Price & Ormel (2026).

sections.body: Planets form in rotating discs of gas and dust around young stars. Some of these discs continue to receive fresh gas from their surroundings, changing their shape and the motion of gas within them. This process is called infall. My recent work explores what happens when that incoming gas reaches a disc, and how we can recognise its effects through a telescope.

What happens when a stream hits a disc?

In Anatomy of a Fall, my collaborators and I used three-dimensional simulations to follow a narrow stream of gas, known as a streamer, colliding with a disc. The encounter launched spiral waves and pushed some gas onto stretched-out orbits.

The spiral patterns behaved in surprising ways. Some barely moved, even while gas flowed through them; others travelled faster than gas on a circular orbit at the same distance from the star. Tracking how spirals move could therefore help identify infall. The effects also outlasted the initial encounter: in our simulation, the disc remained slightly elongated for around 100,000 years.

sections.alt: Six simulation snapshots showing a gas stream meeting a disc and producing spiral arms over time.
sections.caption: Six stages of the simulation, read across the top row, then the bottom. The incoming stream disturbs the disc and leaves spiral patterns behind. Brighter colours show more gas along our line of sight. These are simulated images. Calcino et al. (2025), Figure 1.

sections.body:
Following the gas around AB Aurigae

AB Aurigae is a young star surrounded by a disc with striking spiral arms. It is also receiving fresh gas. In an observational study led by Jessica Speedie, which I coauthored, we traced three streams towards the disc and identified a region where two of them appear to merge with it.

Telescopes can measure gas motion as well as its location. Small shifts in the wavelength of light reveal whether gas is moving towards or away from us. Maps of that motion around AB Aur show bends and wiggles, rather than the smooth pattern expected from gas travelling in circular orbits.

These disturbances had been interpreted as evidence for gravitational instability: a disc so massive that its own gravity helps gather gas into spiral arms. In our follow-up paper on AB Aur, we asked whether infall could produce similar signals. Our simulations recreated key features of the disturbed gas motion without including the gravity of the gas itself.

This means that those signals alone cannot establish whether a disc is gravitationally unstable. Infall offers another explanation. The two processes could also happen together, so our result does not rule out gravitational instability.

Connecting the spirals and the dust ring

We also explored a model combining infall with a second star orbiting inside the disc's central gap. Together, they reproduced many features of AB Aur's spiral pattern and dust ring. The comparison below shows what this model would look like through a telescope. It is a promising explanation, rather than an exact match, and the proposed companion star has not been detected.

sections.alt: Observations of AB Aurigae on the left and simulated telescope images on the right, both showing spiral structure and a ring of dust.
sections.caption: Observations on the left; our model on the right. The coloured images show starlight scattered by dust, while the overlaid contours trace the dust's millimetre emission. Calcino, Price & Ormel (2026), Figure 6. Observational data: Boccaletti et al. (2020) and Speedie et al. (2024, 2025).

sections.body: Understanding how discs respond to their surroundings helps us interpret the structures we see in them. Before attributing a spiral to an unseen planet or to the disc's own gravity, we need to consider the gas arriving from outside.
